transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I'm here today because I've been struggling with severe mental health issues for about two years and five months now. It has been a really difficult mix of deep depression and some very unusual, distressing experiences that make me feel paranoid and unsafe. I just really need some help because it has been going on for so long and I can't cope anymore.
Can you tell me more about these unusual and distressing experiences that make you feel paranoid and unsafe, what exactly happens during these episodes?

It feels like I am constantly being watched and monitored by a specific organization, and they are tracking my every move. No matter where I go, I can feel their eyes on me, and it makes me feel incredibly unsafe and anxious in my own home. I know it sounds hard to believe, but I am certain they are targeting me, and the threat is completely real.

How long have you been experiencing these feelings of being watched, and have you noticed any relationship between these episodes and your depressive symptoms, such as whether one seems to trigger or worsen the other?

I've been feeling watched for about eight months during this current stretch, though my overall struggles began about two and a half years ago. While my depression and these paranoid feelings often happen at the same time, they don't always trigger each other. In fact, I've had periods of at least two weeks where I felt watched and heard things even when I wasn't feeling depressed at all.
You mentioned hearing things, can you describe what you hear during these episodes, and how often these auditory experiences occur in relation to your feelings of being watched?

I usually hear low whispering or voices talking about me in the background, which makes the feeling of being watched so much more intense and terrifying. These voices and the paranoia almost always happen together, making me feel completely unsafe, though there are still times I feel watched even when everything is quiet.

Can you estimate how much of the total duration of your mental health struggles, about two and a half years, has been dominated by depressive symptoms versus these psychotic experiences, and how have these symptoms impacted your daily functioning and relationships?

The depression has definitely been there for the vast majority of these two years and five months, even when the paranoia and voices aren't as active. It has completely ruined my daily life and relationships because I've lost all my motivation to do basic tasks and have entirely withdrawn from everyone around me.

Have there been any periods where you experienced significant depressive symptoms without any psychotic symptoms, such as the feelings of being watched or hearing voices, and if so, how long did those periods last?

Yes, absolutely. For the first year and a half of my struggles, I only had the severe depression without any of the paranoia or voices. Those scary experiences didn't start until about eight months ago.
Can you describe how your depressive symptoms changed, if at all, when the psychotic symptoms, such as the feelings of being watched and hearing voices, first appeared about eight months ago?

When the paranoid feelings and voices started eight months ago, my depression became much more intense and exhausting. Dealing with the constant sadness alongside the terrifying fear of being watched made me feel completely overwhelmed and even more isolated.

Have you experienced any periods of at least two weeks where you had no depressive symptoms, but still experienced psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations, which could help clarify the nature of your condition?

Yes, there have been a few times over the last eight months where my depression lifted and my mood felt relatively normal, but the voices and the feeling of being watched remained just as strong for two or three weeks. It is incredibly exhausting because even when I'm not feeling down, the terror of being monitored never really stops.

Have you experienced any periods of at least two weeks where you had no depressive symptoms, but still experienced psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations, which could help clarify the nature of your condition?

Yes, I have definitely had periods lasting two weeks or more where my depression lifted, but I still heard the whispering and felt like I was being monitored. It’s incredibly exhausting because even when my mood feels relatively normal, the fear and the voices just don't stop.

Have you experienced any periods of at least two weeks where you had no depressive symptoms, but still experienced psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations, which could help clarify the nature of your condition?

Yes, I have definitely experienced times of at least two weeks where my depressive symptoms, like the deep sadness and lack of motivation, were completely gone or much better. Even during those times when my mood felt normal, the voices and the terrifying feeling of being watched remained just as strong.

latest_inference.note: The patient's description of experiencing persistent delusions of being watched and auditory hallucinations, alongside significant depressive symptoms, suggests a psychotic disorder. The fact that the psychotic symptoms have occurred for at least two weeks without depressive symptoms indicates that the condition might not solely be a depressive disorder with psychotic features. However, the prominent depressive symptoms that have been present for the majority of the patient's illness suggest that Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type) could also be a strong candidate. Schizophrenia remains a possibility due to the presence of delusions and hallucinations that have occurred independently of depressive episodes. The patient's symptoms do not clearly fit the criteria for other disorders on the list, such as Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features or Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features, given the duration and nature of the psychotic symptoms in relation to the mood symptoms.
